title: Fanned-out draft: a section's later failure rolls back its own paid first attempt off the ledger
claim: In `_draft_one_apart` the per-section session is committed only on the happy path (line 3144). `execute_builtin_section` catches only `TokenCapExceededError` and `ValidationError` (writing.py:423, 436), so a `BudgetExceededError` from `_refuse_what_cannot_be_afforded` (base.py:523-528) or an `ExternalServiceError` from `count_tokens` (anthropic.py:480-481) on attempt 2 leaves the `async with factory() as session` block by exception; the session closes uncommitted and the `agent_runs`/`costs`/artefact rows that `_meter` flushed for the paid attempt 1 (base.py:881-899) are discarded. The engine then commits its *own* session in `_pause`/`_fail` (engine.py:1093-1103, 1105-1137), which never held those rows. The section row was never mutated (`_failed` is not reached), so on resume it is PENDING and is drafted from attempt 1 again, and `spend_so_far` no longer sees the money that triggered the refusal — the guard admits on resume the very call it refused.
evidence: vertical_slice_v1.py:3127-3145 has no try/except and one `session.commit()` after `_draft_one`; `_drafted_apart` (3280-3292) gathers with return_exceptions and re-raises `first_failure`; writing.py:421-440 catches only the two named exceptions; base.py:508-528 runs `count_tokens` and the budget guard before every attempt; the in-place path (`_drafted_in_place`, used by every savepoint-fixtured test) runs on the engine session, where `_fail` commits (engine.py:835-840), so the loss exists only on the production fan-out path.
reproduction: Scripted provider: call 1 for section S returns a draft `validate_draft` refuses; the second `count_tokens` for S raises `ExternalServiceError` (or set the work order cap so attempt 1's spend + projection crosses it). Drive the draft step with a session factory. Assert on a fresh session: `sum(costs.amount_gbp) where job_step_id = draft step and agent_role = 'report_writer'` excludes S's first call (the fake provider's own tally shows it was billed); `report_sections.status` for S is PENDING; resuming drafts S from attempt 1 with `spend_so_far` lower than what was actually spent.
fix_sketch: Wrap the body of `_draft_one_apart` so that on any exception the session commits what was metered (the rows are whole — the failure is not inside a flush) before re-raising, or have `execute_builtin_section` catch `AerError` around attempt N>1 and return `_failed` so the section's own commit runs; add the test above to tests/test_draft_fanout.py.

title: Truncation retry halves the word budget whatever consumed the ceiling, compounds with quick-mode scaling, and a passing half-budget revision replaces the full approved draft
claim: `_after_refused_reply` cuts `policy.word_budget` to half (lines 142-145, 160) on `stop_reason == "max_tokens"` alone, without reading `unusable.response_payload` to see whether any visible text was written. The provider's own diagnosis (anthropic.py:98-103) says the ceiling is usually spent on thinking before a word of output exists, so the ask is halved for a failure unrelated to length. The retry is then validated against the cut policy (line 442, ceiling = 1.25 × half) and any salvage trims to the cut policy's ceiling (lines 729-733 via `_RefusedAttempt.policy`). Under `AnalysisMode.QUICK` the budget is already 0.6× (line 361, evidence.py:89-93), so the retry writes to 0.3× of the declared budget. On the revise path (`revision.py:216-229`) a revision that passes at half budget is `GENERATED`, so `kept` is False and it replaces the approved full-length draft and its claims (`record_draft_claims`, evidence.py:1005) — ADR 0098 protects only a *refused* revision.
evidence: writing.py:142-166, 361, 437-442, 455, 729-733; revision.py:225-228 (`kept = execution.status is not GENERATED and approved.was_generated`); anthropic.py:98-103; ROADMAP.md:231-233 records the halving only as a mechanism that 'still hold[s]', not as a decision for revisions or quick runs; the writer's user message tells the retry the cut is 'so the whole section fits' (writing.py:161-165) even when the first attempt's text was near-empty.
reproduction: Standard run, definition word_budget 700: scripted provider returns `SpentButUnusableError(context={'stop_reason':'max_tokens'})` whose response_payload text block is 40 words, then a 600-word fully-cited draft → second draft refused for length (ceiling 437) and trimmed; assert the published section is ≤437 words. Quick mode: same, assert the retry asks for 210 words. Revise path: draft a 700-word section with claims, record a severity-4 challenge attributed to it, then script the revision as truncation → 340-word passing draft; assert `section.content` word count ≈340 and the disposition is `revised`, i.e. the approved 700-word draft is gone. Nothing in tests/test_revision_loop.py uses max_tokens; TestTruncationCutsTheAsk (test_section_writer.py:1540-1600) runs standard mode and the first draft only.
fix_sketch: Cut only when the truncated reply's visible text exceeds, say, half the budget (read `response_payload['content']` text blocks); never cut below a floor derived from the declared budget; in `revise_challenged_sections` treat a revision written under a cut policy as refused (keep the approved draft) or pass a flag that disables the cut for revisions.

title: red_team: a schema-rejected or truncated adversary reply escapes the one-retry loop and fails the run; resume repeats the identical call with nothing fed back
claim: `run_red_team` calls `agent.run_batch`/`agent.run` inside its attempt loop with no `except` (lines 196-199); the loop's only retry condition is 'every challenge dropped' (line 207). A `SpentButUnusableError` (a max_tokens stop, or a field over its ceiling) is metered by the base agent (base.py:550-557) and propagates through `_red_team` (vertical_slice_v1.py:1727, no try) to the engine, which records the step FAILED and the job FAILED (engine.py:992-994). The refusal is never fed back through `RedTeamInput.problems`, the ceiling is never raised, and a resume re-runs the same payload at the same 16,384-token ceiling — the 'known failure at full price' pattern the writer's P6 fix names (writing.py:114-119). Every other retrying step (writer, briefer, workers) catches `ValidationError` and sends `schema_problems` back.
evidence: red_team.py:184-217; vertical_slice_v1.py:1709-1739; registry: red_team max_output_tokens=16_384 with adaptive thinking and up to 8 × (1,500 + 1,200)-char challenges; agents/red_team.py:55-60 and tests/test_red_team.py:169-187 describe the earlier fatal case as motivation for raising ceilings, and ROADMAP §4 (lines ~953-956) scopes the retry to dropped challenges — neither decides that a truncation should fail the run.
reproduction: Fake provider scripted to raise `SpentButUnusableError(usage=..., context={'stop_reason':'max_tokens','schema':'RedTeamReport'})` for the red_team role once, then answer normally; run the workflow to `red_team`. Observed: job FAILED at red_team, cost row written, `RedTeamOutcome` never recorded; resume re-sends an identical prompt (`problems=[]`) at max_tokens 16_384. No test under tests/ drives a `SpentButUnusableError` through `run_red_team`.
fix_sketch: Catch `ValidationError` in the loop: on attempt 1 set `problems = schema_problems(rejected)`, raise `agent.output_ceiling_tokens` on a max_tokens stop as `_refused_reply` does, and continue; on a second failure return a skipped outcome with the reason rather than raising (the step is advisory to gate 2 the same way briefs are).

title: propose_assumptions: the ADR 0046 opinions call has no failure handling — one unusable reply fails the run
claim: `_propose_opinions` awaits `AssumptionProposalAgent().run(...)` with no except (lines 643-660); its caller (lines 556-565) and the step (`_propose_assumptions`, vertical_slice_v1.py:1374-1383) have none either. evidence: assumption_gate.py:556-565, 643-660 (no try/except anywhere near); vertical_slice_v1.py:1333-1401 (no try/except); grep for `except` in assumption_gate.py finds only ValueError at 312 and KeyError at 721.

title: Custom sections get none of the four salvages, no truncation headroom and no word-budget cut; ADR 0096/0100 titles do not hold for them
claim: `execute_custom_section` runs the shared `validate_draft` (line 164), which refuses a draft for a malformed claim, a repeated gap remark, an unsourced numeral or a length overrun exactly as for a built-in — but on refusal it only feeds `schema_problems` back (lines 157-161) and, after two refusals, marks the section failed (lines 179-187). No call to `salvaged`/`_with_salvage` exists in the module, `output_ceiling_tokens` is never raised on a max_tokens stop, and the `custom_section` role's ceiling is 8,192 (half the writer's), so truncation is more likely there and the retry repeats it at the same ceiling. ADR 0096 ('a malformed claim costs the claim, not the section') and ADR 0100 ('a repeated gap remark costs the remark, not the section') therefore describe only built-ins, and neither ADR nor the module docstring (lines 1-22) records that scope.
evidence: skills/execution.py:127-187 (grep for `salvag`, `TRUNCATION_RETRY_CEILING`, `output_ceiling_tokens`, `_cut_for_retry` returns nothing); sections/writing.py:463-472 and 660-745 implement the salvage for built-ins only; ADR 0057 contains no mention of custom sections; registry custom_section max_output_tokens=8_192 vs report_writer 16_384; vertical_slice_v1.py:3086-3097 routes pinned custom sections to this path in the live workflow.

Observed: `SectionStatus.FAILED`, content None. The same two drafts through `execute_builtin_section` publish with `LENGTH_EDIT_NOTE`/`CLAIM_EDIT_NOTE`.
fix_sketch: Lift `_RefusedAttempt`, `_with_salvage`, `_refused_reply` and `_after_refused_reply` from writing.py into `aer.sections.evidence` (they depend only on the shared policy/evidence types) and call them from both boundaries; otherwise amend ADR 0096/0100 and the module docstring to state the custom path is excluded and why.

title: Research worker retries a truncated reply at the same output ceiling — the 'same truncation paid for twice' the writer was fixed for
claim: On a `ValidationError` whose stop reason is max_tokens, `_salvaged_turn` returns None (the cut JSON does not parse, lines 701-704), `unreadable` is incremented and `schema_problems` feeds back 'say the same thing in fewer words' (lines 571-572); the worker is retried within the round with `worker.output_ceiling_tokens` untouched — the module never sets it. The writer's docstring (writing.py:114-119) calls exactly this 'a known failure at full price — a live run paid for the same truncation twice' and raises the ceiling to 32,768 for the retry. The worker's visible output (≤12 findings × 600 chars plus leads) is a few thousand tokens, so a 16,384 stop is mostly thinking, which 'fewer words' does not reduce; a second truncation raises out (lines 584-592) and `_research` records the topic as a degraded empty report (vertical_slice_v1.py:3013-3040), thinning every section downstream.
evidence: worker.py:554-600, 680-734; no occurrence of `output_ceiling_tokens` in worker.py (it is set only in sections/writing.py:124); registry analysis max_output_tokens=16_384; worker.py:506-510 says the final round, 'with the whole report to write', is the likeliest truncation point.
reproduction: tests/test_research_workers.py:1194 and 1222 script a max_tokens rejection then a good report and assert only the feedback text; extend either to assert `provider.calls[1]['max_tokens'] > provider.calls[0]['max_tokens']` — it fails today. Live: any topic whose final-round report is truncated twice becomes `degraded` with the worker's cost paid twice.
fix_sketch: In `investigate`, on a max_tokens stop set `worker.output_ceiling_tokens = TRUNCATION_RETRY_CEILING` (move the constant to a shared module) before the retry, exactly as `_refused_reply` does; keep MAX_UNREADABLE_REPLIES.

title: The salvage publishes the last refused attempt even when an earlier attempt needs a lighter repair and no confidence cap
claim: `_with_salvage` iterates `reversed(refused)` and returns the first attempt that salvages (lines 287-309). If attempt 1 was refused for length only (fully cited; repair = trim, `LENGTH_EDIT_NOTE`, no confidence cap) and attempt 2 was refused for one unsourced numeral in a multi-sentence field plus length (repair = sentence removal + trim, `NUMERAL_EDIT_NOTE`, confidence capped at 0.5 by `confidence_ceiling`, section_output.py:117-133), the reader gets attempt 2 with a sentence removed and a 0.5 ceiling, while a draft needing only a trim sat in the run's record. The documented decision (docstring and tests/test_section_writer.py:555) covers 'last first when it can be repaired'; the case where the last needs a *heavier* repair than an earlier one is neither discussed nor tested.
evidence: writing.py:281-311 (docstring: 'Where the last attempt is salvageable the behaviour is unchanged'); section_output.py:100-133 (`_UNSOURCED_MATERIAL_EDITS` caps confidence for NUMERAL/CLAIM edits, not LENGTH/GAP); writing.py:506-509 applies the cap.
reproduction: Scripted drafts: first = `_good_draft` with a 30%-over-budget commentary and every numeral covered; second = the same commentary plus one sentence 'Margins improved 42% on the year.' with no claim. Assert today: published content lacks the 42% sentence and `section.confidence == 0.5`; expected under a least-repair policy: first draft trimmed, confidence = the model's own.
fix_sketch: Salvage every refused attempt and choose by repair weight (no cap beats cap; fewer notes beats more), tie-breaking on latest; or at least prefer an earlier attempt when the last attempt's salvage would introduce an `_UNSOURCED_MATERIAL_EDITS` note and the earlier would not.

title: A `refusal` stop reason is retried once at full price in every ladder although the provider's own diagnosis says retrying will not help
claim: `_validated` raises a `ValidationError` for `stop_reason == 'refusal'` with the text 'retrying will not help' (anthropic.py:104-107, 857-866). `schema_problems` has no branch for it and returns the generic 'could not be read as a turn' line (base.py:127-141); the writer (writing.py:436-440), the custom section (skills/execution.py:157-161), the briefer (challenge_briefs.py:183-185) and the worker (worker.py:556-572) all treat that as an ordinary rejection and pay for a second attempt with a message that tells the model nothing about the refusal.

title: Per-call guard cannot see sibling spend: parallel research nodes and fanned-out draft sections each guard against committed spend only, so the per-run cap is jointly overshot
claim: Inside the research wave (five nodes, one session each) and inside the draft step's fan-out (four sections, one session each), every model call's affordability check sums only rows visible to the calling session — rows committed by finished siblings plus its own flushed rows — so N siblings can each pass a check that their combined spend breaks, by up to (N−1) × one call's worst case per round, with no BudgetExceededError.
evidence: base.py:449 `spent = await spend_so_far(context.session, job_id=job.id)`; `_meter` only flushes (base.py:899) and `_meter_search` only flushes (research.py:493). A parallel node's session commits once, at the end of the node (engine.py:789 `await node_session.commit()`); a fanned-out section commits at vertical_slice_v1.py:3144 after its calls. Postgres READ COMMITTED never shows another session's uncommitted rows, so during the wave the five `analysis` workers (up to MAX_ROUNDS calls each, 16,384-token ceiling on claude-sonnet-5) and during the draft the four `report_writer` sections (16,384-token ceiling on claude-opus-5 ≈ £0.32 output + input per call) each price against a total that omits every sibling still running. The engine's wave-level `in_flight` (engine.py:653-690) adds only step *estimates*, once, before the nodes start; nothing inside a step reads a sibling. ADR 0053 states 'the last call of a long step is guarded exactly as its first, against spend that includes everything the step has already metered' — not true under the wave or under DRAFT_FAN_OUT (added later, P10); the comment at vertical_slice_v1.py:290-297 admits the window ('every section in flight checks the cap against the same total') but no ADR records it, and the same window applies across two runs executing concurrently on the monthly cap (spend_this_month, engine.py:347-362).
reproduction: With a session factory (the ARQ path, tests/test_draft_fanout.py `metered_driver(parallel=True)`): seed a work order whose cap leaves £0.50 of headroom before the draft step's four sections start; give the fake provider per-section usage costing £0.30 and a delay so all four are in flight together. Expect: all four sections complete, `sum(costs.amount_gbp)` for the job ends ≈ £0.70 over `work_orders.max_cost_gbp`, and no step row carries `budget_exceeded`. Same construction on the research wave with five workers.
fix_sketch: Either commit cost rows as they are written (a short savepoint/commit per `_meter`, which the step-boundary publication rule already tolerates for sections), or reserve in-flight worst cases in a shared place the guard reads (a `reservations` table or Redis key per job keyed by call id, released on meter), or bound concurrency so that (fan_out − 1) × worst case is added to `projected_gbp` in `_refuse_what_cannot_be_afforded`. Record the chosen window in an ADR amending 0053.

title: raise_cap is not seen by the per-call guard until the run is resumed: it reads the work order through the identity map of a session that never expires
claim: The per-call guard reads the per-run cap with `session.get(WorkOrder, …)`, which returns the already-loaded instance without a query; the worker's sessions are `expire_on_commit=False` and the work order is loaded at the start of every execution/node/section, so a cap raised from the web process mid-run is invisible to every model call until the run stops and is resumed — contradicting raise_cap's docstring and the test that was written to prove the raise takes effect at the next step.
evidence: base.py:436-438 `job = await context.session.get(Job, …)`; `work_order = … await context.session.get(WorkOrder, job.work_order_id)`; base.py:456 `cap=Decimal(str(work_order.max_cost_gbp))`. `ResearchRequest.work_order` is `lazy="joined"` (db/models/request.py:146), and the request is loaded into the session before anything runs: runs.py:197 `mandate_of(session, job)` on the serial session, vertical_slice_v1.py:3788-3789 `_request_for` in every node, vertical_slice_v1.py:3129 `session.get(ResearchRequest, …)` per fanned-out section. worker.py:198 `async_sessionmaker(engine, expire_on_commit=False)` — the commits at every `_publish` leave the cached WorkOrder unexpired. SQLAlchemy `Session.get` returns the identity-map object with no SQL unless it is expired. The engine's BudgetGuard reads a bare column select (engine.py:292-294) and does see the raise; tests/test_cap_raise.py:161-180 tests only that guard, and on the *same* session that performed the raise. requests.py:582-583 claims 'both spend guards re-read it before every step and every model call'; the console's remedy 'Raise the cap on this request to continue' (base.py:457) therefore does not continue the run.
reproduction: Seed a job with cap £1.00 and £0.90 spent (as tests/test_cap_raise.py). On session A (`async_sessionmaker(engine, expire_on_commit=False)`): `await session_a.get(ResearchRequest, request_id)` (loads the WorkOrder), then in session B call `request_service.raise_cap(..., to=Decimal('2.00'))` and commit. Back on session A run `_Probe().run(context, 'Brief.')` with a call whose worst case is £0.30: BudgetExceededError is raised with `context['cap_gbp'] == '1.00'` although `select(WorkOrder.max_cost_gbp)` on session A returns 2.00. Live: raise the cap during the research wave and watch the next worker call pause the run at the old figure.
fix_sketch: Read the cap the way the engine does — `await context.session.scalar(select(WorkOrder.max_cost_gbp).where(WorkOrder.id == job.work_order_id))` — or `await context.session.refresh(work_order, ['max_cost_gbp'])` before comparing; add the two-session test above. Consider having both guards share one `per_run_cap(session, job)` helper so they cannot diverge again.

title: A routable model outside the price table is priced at Opus-5 rates, which under-prices Fable-tier models by half (meter and per-call projection alike)
claim: `unknown_model_prices` returns the dearest *listed* model (claude-opus-5, $5/$25), but the provider explicitly accepts routes to `claude-fable-5` (and the API serves `claude-fable-5-1`), which cost $10/$50; an operator who routes any role there gets every call metered at half its bill and every per-call worst case projected at half, so both caps admit twice the money they name and the /costs page understates the run — the opposite of the docstring's 'the safe error is to overstate it'.
evidence: costs.py:79-86 DEFAULT_PRICES lists only claude-opus-5, claude-sonnet-5, claude-haiku-4-5; costs.py:147 `return max(DEFAULT_PRICES.values(), key=lambda p: p.output_usd)`; costs.py:163 and 243 fall back to it for `price_usage` and `estimate_gbp`. anthropic.py:82-92 `_MODELS_ACCEPTING_EFFORT` includes 'claude-fable-5' (and opus-4-8/4-7/4-6, sonnet-4-6), i.e. the provider is built to route there; `AER_MODEL_ROUTES` (config.py:381-383) accepts any model string with no check against the price table. Published first-party rates (claude-api skill, cached 2026-06-24): Fable 5 / Fable 5.1 $10.00 in / $50.00 out per MTok, Opus 5 $5/$25. The fallback also mis-states cache rates for those models (derived from the Opus input rate).

title: A call that fails after the request was accepted (stream disconnect, read timeout) is not metered: the accumulated usage is discarded with the exception
claim: When `messages.stream(...)`/`get_final_message()` raises after `message_start` — a mid-stream disconnect or a 600 s read timeout while the model thinks — the vendor has billed the full input and the output generated so far, but the error carries no usage, `Agent.run` meters only `SpentButUnusableError`, and no `costs` row is written; the resumed step then spends again, so the ledger under-counts by one call's cost per event.
evidence: anthropic.py:238-243: `async with self._client.messages.stream(...) as stream: response = await stream.get_final_message()` inside `except Exception as exc: raise _api_failure(...)` — `_api_failure` (anthropic.py:1110-1144) builds an ExternalServiceError with no usage; `stream.current_message_snapshot` (which carries `usage.input_tokens` from message_start and the partial output count) is never read. base.py:550-557 meters only `SpentButUnusableError`; ExternalServiceError propagates to `_run_node`/`_execute` and the step fails with nothing on the ledger. The docstring at anthropic.py:193-204 records the live disconnect history (three minutes in, every time, pre-streaming) but neither it nor an ADR records that such a call is unmetered. Worst case per event: one call's input plus up to 16,384 output tokens on claude-opus-5 (≈ £0.32 output alone).
reproduction: Unit: stub `messages.stream` so `get_final_message` raises `httpx.RemoteProtocolError` after a snapshot with `usage.input_tokens=50_000` is available on `current_message_snapshot`; call `provider.complete_structured` and assert the raised error carries usage (today it does not), then assert `Agent.run` wrote cost rows (today none). Live: compare the Anthropic console's token totals with `sum(costs.amount_usd)` for a run whose step row records `external_service_error` after a stream failure.
fix_sketch: In the `except` branch read `stream.current_message_snapshot.usage` when present and raise a usage-carrying error (a `SpentButUnusableError`-like subclass of ExternalServiceError), and meter it in `Agent.run`'s failure path; add a test for the stream-broken-after-message_start case. Consider `max_retries=0` in `_build_client` for the non-streamed search call so a timed-out request is not silently re-sent and double-billed.

title: A web search that the vendor's tool refuses still bills the carrying call's tokens, which are discarded rather than metered
claim: When the search result block is an error object, `search_web` raises after the message(s) completed; the vendor waives only the per-search fee, not the tokens of the response, but the executor records a refusal with no cost row — and a test enshrines the omission.
evidence: anthropic.py:522-534 collects `usages` from every `messages.create` (the API returned HTTP 200 with `usage`), then anthropic.py:538-548 raises ExternalServiceError on `error is not None` without carrying them; a raise inside the `pause_turn` loop (anthropic.py:529-534) likewise drops the first call's usage. research.py:410-418 turns the error into a refusal and skips `_meter_search`, citing 'A failed search is not billed — the vendor's published rule' — the rule quoted in ADR 0092 (`the web search will not be billed`) is about the search unit; standard token costs are separately stated as 'plus standard token costs'. tests/test_web_search.py:171-181 asserts `_costs(...) == []` for this case. Magnitude is small (claude-haiku-4-5, max_tokens 2048, ≤3 searches per worker) but it is a spent-and-unmetered path.
reproduction: Stub a `web_search_tool_result` error block on a response with `usage.input_tokens=200, output_tokens=50` (as tests/test_web_search.py:290-298 does) and run the executor: no `costs` row is written for 250 billed tokens. Compare against the console's token count for a run whose worker logged `The web search failed:`.
fix_sketch: Carry the collected usages on the raised error (or return an outcome with `hits=()`, `searches=0` and an `error` field) and meter the token lines in `_web_search` before returning the refusal; drop only the fee line. Update the test at test_web_search.py:171 to assert token rows exist and no `web_search` fee row does.

title: Web searches bypass the per-call affordability guard: a run at its ceiling can still spend on searches
claim: `_web_search` calls `provider.search_web` directly, never `_refuse_what_cannot_be_afforded`, so the only money check on a search is the worker step's estimate at step start; once a worker is running, up to three searches per node (fee + a claude-haiku-4-5 call with max_tokens 2048) are made regardless of remaining headroom — about £0.02 each, ≤ £0.30 per run past either cap across five workers.
evidence: research.py:406-409 `outcome = await agent_context.provider.search_web(...)` with no budget call before it; the per-call guard lives only in `Agent.run`/`run_batch` (base.py:523-528, 635-640). anthropic.py:504-520 sets `max_tokens: 2048` on the carrying call. ADR 0053: 'Every call is priced before it is made, and the price is checked against both real ceilings'; ADR 0092 relies on the step estimate ('the per-worker step estimate covers the bounded searches'), which is checked once, before the node starts (engine.py:658-665).
reproduction: Seed a job whose spend equals its cap exactly (guard uses `total <= cap`, base.py:486), build executors with a search-capable FakeProvider (tests/test_web_search.py scene) and call `executors['web_search'](_tool_request())`: it executes and writes cost rows taking the run over its cap; a probe `Agent.run` on the same context is refused.
fix_sketch: Before `search_web`, project the search's worst case (fee + `estimate_gbp(model=route.model, input_tokens≈query, expected_output_tokens=2048)`) through the same `_refuse_over_ceiling` helper (expose it as a module function) and return a refusal naming the scope; add the test above.

title: The per-call 'worst case' prices input at the uncached rate although every call requests a cache write, which bills at 1.25× input
claim: `_refuse_what_cannot_be_afforded` projects `input_tokens × input_usd + ceiling × output_usd`, but the provider marks the system block and any stable prefix `cache_control: ephemeral` on every request, so on a cold cache those tokens are billed at `cache_write_usd = 1.25 × input_usd`; the projection can understate the call by 25% of its input cost (a 100k-token claude-opus-5 prompt: $0.50 projected, $0.625 billed, ≈ £0.10), so the guard's 'worst case' is not the worst case.
evidence: base.py:424-429 → costs.py:245-248 `Decimal(input_tokens) * model_prices.input_usd + …`; anthropic.py:650-660 `_system_blocks` marks the system prompt unconditionally and anthropic.py:663-673 marks `cache_prefix`; costs.py:75 `cache_write_usd=base * Decimal('1.25')` and costs.py:169 meters `CACHE_WRITE` at that rate. ADR 0053 §'The projection deliberately ignores prompt caching' argues only that hits must not be assumed; it does not consider that a write costs more than uncached. tests/test_providers.py:242-257 proves estimate == meter only for usage with no cache tokens.
reproduction: `uv run python -c "from decimal import Decimal; from aer.providers.costs import estimate_gbp, price_usage, total_gbp; from aer.providers.protocol import Usage; e=estimate_gbp(model='claude-opus-5', input_tokens=100_000, expected_output_tokens=0, usd_to_gbp=Decimal(1)); m=total_gbp(price_usage(Usage(input_tokens=0, output_tokens=0, cache_write_tokens=100_000, model='claude-opus-5'), provider='anthropic', usd_to_gbp=Decimal(1))); print(e, m)"` prints 0.50 0.625.
fix_sketch: Price projected input at `cache_write_usd` in `estimate_gbp` (or add a `worst_case=True` flag used by the guard), and extend test_providers.py with a property: for any usage the guard's projection of (input+cache_write tokens, output ceiling) ≥ the metered total.

title: Cost rows are flushed, not committed, inside a step: a step whose session is rolled back or whose worker dies loses every metered call of that attempt
claim: `_meter`/`_meter_search` only flush; the first commit is at the end of the node, section or step. `_record_node_failure` rolls the session back when the failure commit is refused — discarding the attempt's cost rows with the rest — and a worker killed mid-node leaves the same rows uncommitted; on resume the step spends again and only the second attempt reaches the ledger, so the monthly total is under-counted by the lost attempt's spend.
evidence: base.py:899 `await context.session.flush()`; research.py:493 flush; engine.py:789 `node_session.commit()` after `step.run`; vertical_slice_v1.py:3144 per-section commit; engine.py:1000 `_publish` after the serial step. engine.py:840-848: on `SQLAlchemyError` from the failure commit, `await node_session.rollback()` — the docstring (engine.py:820-823) says the rollback 'discards whatever the step had written before it broke', which includes its `costs` rows, but neither it, `_publish`'s docstring (engine.py:875-903) nor an ADR records the ledger consequence. The acceptance pass (docs/plan/acceptance-2026-09-08.md:32 'a killed worker resumes') did not check the killed attempt's spend.
reproduction: Run a research node under the ARQ worker with a fake provider that meters £0.10 per call and raise inside `_meter` after two flushed calls with an IntegrityError on the third (or SIGKILL the worker mid-node): after resume, `select sum(amount_gbp) from costs where job_id=…` omits the first attempt's £0.20 although `agent.completed` log lines and the vendor console show them.
fix_sketch: Commit cost rows in their own short transaction (a dedicated session from the factory, or `begin_nested` + commit at `_meter`) so a metered call is durable the moment it is priced; in `_record_node_failure`, salvage the flushed Cost rows before `rollback()` and re-add them. Add a test that a node failing after two metered calls still leaves two cost rows.

title: Batch-endpoint results are priced at list rates although the Batches API bills at 50%: the ledger cannot reconcile to the vendor's bill (off the vertical_slice run path today)
claim: `price_usage` has no notion of transport, so items returned by `complete_structured_batch` from the real Batches API are metered at 2× what the vendor charges; the module docstring's promise that the ledger reconciles against the vendor's bill does not hold for batched calls. Within vertical_slice_v1 the batch endpoint is never actually reached (the red team sends one item, which the provider routes to the single path), so today only `services/evaluations.py` is affected — but that spend still counts against the monthly cap at double.
evidence: costs.py:150-190 prices by category and model only; base.py:665-676 meters batch results through the same `_meter`; anthropic.py:329-340 sends a single item down the single-call path, and `services/red_team.py:197` calls `run_batch(context, [payload])` with one item; `services/evaluations.py:707` batches many. docs/archive/PLAN.md:232 records 'Batch API | 50% discount'; costs.py:15-19 and 200-205 state the reconciliation requirement. No ADR records pricing batches at list rate.
reproduction: Run an evaluation that submits ≥2 items to the real Batches API and compare `sum(costs.amount_usd)` for that job against the Anthropic console's batch charges: the ledger shows twice the bill.
fix_sketch: Give `StructuredResult`/`Usage` a `batch: bool` (or `rate_multiplier`) set by the batch path and apply 0.5 in `price_usage`; document the multiplier on the cost row (e.g. `unit_type='tokens(batch)'`) so old rows stay interpretable. Add a pricing test for batch usage.

title: The data_api category is never written and cost.py's docstring describes a row nothing creates; acquisition spend is off the ledger by design but undocumented
claim: Only two code paths construct `Cost` rows (token lines and web-search fees); `CostCategory.DATA_API` has no writer. The docstring's 'A data-provider fee belongs to the job with no step' describes a shape that never occurs. EODHD acquisition is metered only as a weighted daily call allowance in Redis (units, not money), so the ledger and both caps see £0 for every price/fundamentals fetch; SEC, Companies House and FRED are free. Nothing in docs/adr or the ROADMAP records that data-subscription spend is intentionally outside the ledger.
evidence: `grep -rn 'Cost(' src/aer` → base.py:883 and research.py:479 only; costs.py:106 `DATA_API = 'data_api'` unreferenced elsewhere; cost.py:13-16 and 55. sources/eodhd/budget.py:1-36, 146-181 reserves weighted calls against DAILY_WEIGHTED_CALLS in Redis and never touches `costs`. ROADMAP.md:1148-1151 mentions 'multiplies the data subscription across the set' as a pending decision without stating how it is metered.

fix_sketch: Either record the decision (an ADR or a knowledge-map line: 'subscription data has zero marginal cost and is bounded by the provider's daily allowance, not the ledger') and correct cost.py's docstring, or write a zero-amount `data_api` row per EODHD request (units = weighted calls) so the run's acquisition footprint is auditable alongside its model spend.

title: Nothing proves the per-run cap holds across concurrent nodes or fanned-out sections
claim: The fan-out test asserts the step's recorded cost equals the sum of metered rows, and the DAG test asserts only the wave-start estimate check; no test starts N concurrent sections/nodes whose individual calls fit the cap but whose sum does not, and asserts a BUDGET_EXCEEDED pause before the cap is passed.

title: A wave failure is silently dropped when an independent branch then pauses on the serial path
claim: After a parallel node fails, `run()` keeps scheduling and stores the exception in `first_failure` (lines 570-571), but the serial path's two early returns — `if paused: return outputs` (545-546) and the step-mode return (550-551) — exit without raising it or setting the job FAILED; only the fall-through at 573-578 does. The job ends AWAITING_APPROVAL with a FAILED step row nobody is shown, and the failed step is re-executed automatically on the next approval, with no `run.resumed` audit event.
evidence: engine.py:545-551 return `outputs` directly; 573-578 is the only place `first_failure` is raised. Module docstring 43-45 promises "an independent branch completes and keeps its work before the failure is re-raised". In the real graph (vertical_slice_v1.py:482-515) a failure of `acquire_prices` in the seven-node wave abandons only `comps` and `draft`; `propose_assumptions` (needs calculate + research×5) is then the sole ready node, runs serially, and `gate_assumptions` (chain after it, 545-549) raises StepPaused via `_require_approval` (2150-2155). `_acquire_prices` can raise: `_record_listing` calls `client.fetch_bars` with no exception handling (services/price_acquisition.py:423). The console hides the failure because `failed` is only derived when `job.status is FAILED` (web/pages.py:418-422). On approval, `execute` re-enters: the FAILED prices row is not SUCCEEDED so it is re-executed in a wave alongside the gate (engine.py:513, 554-561).
reproduction: Engine test with a session factory: steps a; b(needs a, raises RuntimeError); c(needs a); g(needs c, raises StepPaused). Run and assert `pytest.raises(RuntimeError)` and job FAILED — today `run()` returns normally with job.status AWAITING_APPROVAL and rows b=FAILED, g=AWAITING_APPROVAL. Workflow-level: monkeypatch `vertical_slice_v1._acquire_prices` to raise, drive through gate_unmapped_concepts with a factory; observe status AWAITING_APPROVAL at gate_assumptions and no banner on /runs/{id}.
fix_sketch: In `run()`, before both serial early returns, if `first_failure is not None` set job FAILED, publish and raise (or return a paused status only when nothing has failed); add the test above.

title: A step that raises after flushing rows has those rows committed with its FAILED status; render becomes unrecoverable
claim: `_record_node_failure`'s ordinary branch commits the failing step's session as-is (832-838), so every row the step flushed before raising a non-database exception is published alongside `status=FAILED`. For `render`, that commits a `reports` row for a failed run; because `reports.job_id` is unique, every subsequent resume re-runs `_render`, inserts a second Report and fails on the constraint, while `start_run` refuses a fresh run because a report exists. The run cannot be completed, resumed or superseded.
evidence: engine.py:832-838: `get(JobStep)` then `commit()` with the step's pending state still in the session (rollback happens only on SQLAlchemyError, 840-848). vertical_slice_v1.py:3712-3730 adds and flushes the Report; 3737 `record_confirmed_themes`, 3749 `store.read`, 3750 `render_pdf` (a GTK/WeasyPrint stack the comment at 3741-3746 itself calls fragile) and 3756 `store_artefact` all run after the flush and can raise. db/models/report.py:55 `job_id … unique=True`. runs.py:172-175 `_may_be_superseded` returns False when a Report row exists. web/pages.py:234,257 shows the "Read the report" link from `select(Report).where(Report.job_id == job_id)` regardless of job status. This contradicts `_publish`'s own contract (engine.py:878-882: "a reader sees a finished step or no step") and ADR 0016 §"The step is the unit of publication".
reproduction: Take a run through gate_final approval; monkeypatch `aer.render.pdf.render_pdf` to raise RuntimeError; run the worker. Observe: job FAILED, a committed `reports` row with `pdf_artefact_id IS NULL` and `immutable = true`, console offers "Read the report". Then `aer resume <job>` (or POST /runs/{id}/resume): `_render` raises IntegrityError on `reports_job_id_key`; job FAILED again on every attempt; POST /runs (start afresh) returns the same job.
fix_sketch: In `_fail`/`_record_node_failure`, roll back the step's pending work before recording the failure on a clean transaction (the row and job ids are already held for exactly this), so a failed step publishes nothing but its FAILED row; additionally make `_render` re-entrant by reusing an existing Report for the job. Test: a step that adds and flushes a row then raises — assert the row is absent after the failure is recorded.

title: Cost rows are lost when a step dies mid-flight or poisons its session, so both caps under-count real spend
claim: Model spend is recorded with `session.add(Cost(...))` + `flush()` and never committed inside a step, so a worker that dies mid-step (a research worker or `revise` runs for minutes and many calls) leaves no cost row for money the provider has already billed; and `_record_node_failure`'s rollback branch deliberately discards the same rows for a step that fails inside a flush. `spend_so_far`/`spend_this_month` then under-count, and the per-run and monthly guards admit spend that has already happened. Invariant 6 ("every model call … writes a cost row") does not hold across either event.
evidence: agents/base.py:882-899 and services/research.py:477-493 add and flush only; engine.py:875-903 documents that no commit happens inside a step; engine.py:848 `await node_session.rollback()` after a poisoned failure, with the docstring at 821-823 accepting the loss of "whatever the step had written". Guards read committed rows only: engine.py:347-374. Exposure per event is one step's spend: REVISE_ESTIMATE_GBP £1.50 (vertical_slice_v1.py:257), WORKER_ESTIMATE_GBP £0.30 per research node, and up to DRAFT_FAN_OUT=4 in-flight sections in `draft` (only completed sections commit, 3144). Test gap: test_workflow_dag.py:392-420 asserts only FAILED statuses after the poison, never that the step's costs survived.
reproduction: Step test: call `_meter`-equivalent (add a Cost for the job, flush) then perform the duplicate-Prompt flush from test_workflow_dag.py:403-411 so the session is poisoned; after `run()` raises, `SELECT sum(amount_gbp) FROM costs WHERE job_id = :id` is 0 although a model call was billed. Worker-death variant: kill the worker during `revise`; the `costs` table has no rows for that step's attempt.
fix_sketch: Meter on a separate short-lived session (or savepoint + commit of cost rows only) so a cost row is durable the moment usage is known; on the rollback path, re-insert the cost rows captured from `agent_context` before recording the failure. Test both.

title: A worker that dies mid-step leaves the job RUNNING with no supported way out, and the console cannot tell
claim: After a worker crash the job stays RUNNING in Postgres: arq keeps the queue entry in progress for job_timeout+10 s (7210 s) and then fails it as "max retries exceeded" without touching the job row. `resume_run` refuses RUNNING, `start_run` refuses to supersede a non-terminal job, cancellation only writes a row that no executing engine will read, and approvals need a pending gate. The web console consults worker health only for QUEUED jobs, so a dead run shows a green elapsed clock indefinitely; `aer diagnose` reports it correctly only while no worker at all is alive — after a worker restart it prints a green "alive … 0 job(s) ongoing" for a job that will never move. The one command that executes a RUNNING job, `aer step`, does so by accident of its status checks and is not offered as the remedy.
evidence: runs.py:202-207 sets RUNNING and commits. .venv/…/arq/worker.py:277 `in_progress_timeout_s = max_timeout + 10`; 549-561 `job_try > max_tries` → JobExecutionFailed; worker.py:66 `_MAX_TRIES = 1`, 61 `_JOB_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 7200`. resume.py:35 and 56-66 refuse RUNNING. runs.py:172 `_may_be_superseded` returns False for non-terminal. cancellation.py:56-69 writes a row only; engine.py:501 reads it only inside `run()`. web/pages.py:279 `_queued_words` only when `status is QUEUED`; console.html:380-384 remedy is "look at the terminal running just worker"; api/sse.py heartbeat never consults worker health. cli.py:1965-1976 (no health, RUNNING) says "check the worker terminal" with no action; 1989-1992 prints green for RUNNING + live idle worker. cli.py:1704-1713 `_step_once` resumes only FAILED, then `set_step_mode` (refuses terminal only) and `execute` on a RUNNING job. ROADMAP.md:268-269 and 761-763 claim "that is how a run survives the worker dying" — true of the step rows, not of the job. ADR 0016 records the missing sweep for the step row only; the job-level dead end is not a recorded decision.
reproduction: Start a run, kill the worker (SIGKILL) during `research_company`, restart the worker. Observe: job RUNNING; POST /runs/{id}/resume → 409 "It is running now"; POST /runs (same request) → returns the same job; console shows a running clock; `aer diagnose <job>` prints "worker: alive — … 0 job(s) ongoing" in green; after 7210 s arq logs "max retries exceeded" and Redis' health record shows j_failed +1 while Postgres still says RUNNING. Test to write: `worker_words(health=WorkerHealth(ongoing=0,…), status=RUNNING)` should not be green.
fix_sketch: Detect the orphan (health record present with `ongoing == 0`, or absent, while a job is RUNNING) on the console and in `aer diagnose`, and offer a recorded transition — e.g. `resume_run` accepting RUNNING when no worker reports an ongoing job, or a `run.orphaned` audit event that moves the job to FAILED so the existing resume path applies; record the decision in an ADR amending 0090.

title: Cancelling a paused or queued-without-worker run records a request that nothing will ever act on
claim: `request_cancellation` accepts any non-terminal status but only writes a `job_cancellations` row; the engine honours it solely at a scheduling boundary during execution. A run stopped at a gate (AWAITING_APPROVAL), in step mode (PAUSED), at the budget (BUDGET_EXCEEDED) or QUEUED with no worker is not executing, so the cancellation never lands: the job stays non-terminal, the console says "Stopping — the run stops at the end of the step it is in", the cancel form disappears, and for AWAITING_APPROVAL the resume button is hidden too. The only ways to make the cancellation take effect are to approve the gate the operator wanted to stop at, or to press "Continue this run".
evidence: cancellation.py:56-69 (status check is terminal-only; no status change); engine.py:496-503 is the only reader. console.html:170-189 banner text; 392 hides the cancel form once a cancellation exists; web/pages.py:455-457 `can_resume` excludes AWAITING_APPROVAL and QUEUED. Consequences while stuck: runs.py:149-160 `current_run` keeps pointing at it, runs.py:172 refuses a new run for the request, runs.py:454-459 keeps counting it in the approvals badge. Tests: test_cancellation.py:151-212 always run the engine immediately after requesting; no test cancels a job whose status is AWAITING_APPROVAL/PAUSED/BUDGET_EXCEEDED.
reproduction: Drive a run to gate_plan (AWAITING_APPROVAL). POST /runs/{id}/cancel → 303; GET /runs/{id}: status still AWAITING_APPROVAL, banner "Stopping", no cancel or continue form; approvals badge still 1; POST /runs for the request returns the same job. Nothing changes however long you wait. Test to write: request_cancellation on an AWAITING_APPROVAL job, then assert some supported action reaches CANCELLED without approving the gate.
fix_sketch: When the job is not RUNNING (and, for QUEUED, no worker reports it ongoing), have `request_cancellation` — or the route — apply the transition immediately: set CANCELLED + finished_at and publish, with the same audit event; keep the deferred path for RUNNING. Or have the console offer "Continue" as the honest remedy with wording that says continuing will stop it.

title: The same job can be enqueued twice and `execute` accepts any status, so a failed step is re-run and paid for without a decision
claim: Both start-run handlers enqueue unconditionally even when `start_run` returned the existing, still-live job; `_enqueue` passes no `_job_id` so arq does not de-duplicate; and `execute` sets RUNNING and runs the engine whatever the job's status. With one worker the second queued execution runs after the first stops: if the first ended FAILED, the failed step is re-executed and re-billed with no `run.resumed` audit event — the automatic retry that `_MAX_TRIES = 1` and ADR 0090 ("crash recovery — no event — nothing was decided") rule out. With two worker processes (which worker.py records has happened) the same step executes concurrently on the same reused RUNNING row, both attempts spend, and the last commit wins the output.
evidence: web/pages.py:185-187 and api/routes/runs.py:182-185 call `enqueue_run` after `start_run`; runs.py:92-94 returns the existing job when it is not terminal-without-report. queue.py:138 `pool.enqueue_job(task_name, str(identifier))` with no `_job_id`. runs.py:202 `job.status = JobStatus.RUNNING` with no guard; `resume_run`'s RUNNING refusal (resume.py:35) is the only guard and it is not on the execution path. engine.py:1042-1058 reuses the single step row and increments `attempt` for whoever arrives; db/models/job_step.py:90 uniqueness is on (job_id, step_key, attempt), which does not stop two processes updating the same row. worker.py:248 `max_jobs = 1` serialises within one process only; worker.py:202-205 documents two workers serving one run. Test gap: test_run_api.py:222-225 asserts the same job id for two starts but not the number of enqueues.
reproduction: POST /api/runs twice for one request (or click Start twice); with the fake queue in tests, `enqueued.job_ids.count(job_id) == 2`. Then let the planner raise: after the first execution records FAILED, the worker immediately runs the second queued entry: the plan step's `attempt` becomes 1, a second planner call is billed, and no `run.resumed` audit event exists. Two-worker variant: start two `arq` processes and observe both write `attempt` on the same `job_steps` row.
fix_sketch: Have `execute` refuse a job that is RUNNING, SUCCEEDED or CANCELLED (mirror of `UNRESUMABLE_STATUSES`) and log/skip rather than run; only enqueue from the start handlers when `start_run` created a new job (or the job is QUEUED); optionally give arq a deterministic `_job_id` per (job, decision/resume event) so a duplicate click cannot double-queue.

title: A retried step keeps its previous attempt's finished_at, output_ref and cost while RUNNING
claim: When `_step_row` reuses an existing row it resets `status`, `attempt`, `started_at` and `error` but not `finished_at`, `output_ref` or `cost_gbp`. During the retry the row says RUNNING with a `finished_at` earlier than `started_at`, the old output and the old cost, so the diagnostic's `elapsed_seconds` is negative and the timeline shows a stale cost/output for a step that is mid-flight.
evidence: engine.py:1051-1058 (fields reset); 996-999 is the only place `finished_at`/`output_ref`/`cost_gbp` are written on success. services/step_diagnostic.py:78-82 computes `finished_at - started_at` whenever both are set; runs.py:372-381 copies `cost_gbp` and `finished_at` into the timeline entry.
reproduction: Run a step to FAILED (row has finished_at, cost_gbp), resume, and read the row while the retry is in flight: status RUNNING, started_at > finished_at, `StepReadout.elapsed_seconds < 0`. Test: assert `finished_at is None` and `cost_gbp == 0` on a RUNNING row after `_step_row` reuses it.
fix_sketch: In the reuse branch set `existing.finished_at = None`, `existing.output_ref = None`, `existing.cost_gbp = Decimal(0)` alongside the other resets.

title: Nothing exercises seven nodes at the bound of seven, or an eighth being held
claim: The engine's bound is correct in code, but the only load test runs eight free nodes at `max_parallel=3` and the only bound test checks the constructor's refusal of 0 and 8. The real workflow's post-extraction wave is exactly seven nodes at the default bound; no test asserts that all seven start in one wave (high-water 7), that an eighth ready node is deferred to the next round, or that the budget guard's in-flight sum is applied across a full seven-node wave.
evidence: tests/test_workflow_dag.py:471-480 (`max_parallel=3`, `high_water <= 3`); 160-165 (constructor only). engine.py:89 `MAX_PARALLEL_NODES = 7`, 429-434 range check, 557 `ready[: self._max_parallel]`, 658-690 in-flight budget sum. vertical_slice_v1.py:482-515 declares seven nodes needing `gate_unmapped_concepts`.
reproduction: Add a Tracker test with 8 free nodes at the default bound: assert `high_water == 7`, `len(finished) == 8`, and that the eighth node started only after the wave drained; add a variant with five costed nodes where the sixth's `in_flight + estimate` crosses the cap and assert it did not start.
fix_sketch: Two tests in TestParallelNodes as described.

title: A rejected gate leaves the run AWAITING_APPROVAL for ever, with no supported exit but cancel-then-continue
claim: `_require_approval` treats a REJECTED decision as another StepPaused, so the job returns to AWAITING_APPROVAL; a second decision is refused, superseding is refused because the job is non-terminal, and cancellation only writes a row (finding above). The operator's only path to a fresh run is to cancel and then press "Continue this run" so the engine can honour the cancellation — which the console does not say.
evidence: vertical_slice_v1.py:2157-2161 raises StepPaused on a non-APPROVED decision; services/approvals.py references JobStatus only at line 247 (no job transition on rejection); web/pages.py:1802-1803 enqueues only on APPROVED; runs.py:172 refuses supersede for non-terminal; console.html:73 mentions rejecting but no template text covers the rejected state; no test named for a rejected gate's aftermath in tests/test_run_api.py, tests/test_web_gates.py or tests/test_gates.py.
reproduction: Reject gate_plan via POST /runs/{id}/gates/PLAN with decision=REJECTED. GET /runs/{id}: AWAITING_APPROVAL, no pending gate action, no continue form. POST /runs for the request → same job. Only cancel + resume reaches CANCELLED. Test: after a rejection assert the job reaches a terminal state or the console offers a path to one.
fix_sketch: On a REJECTED decision, transition the job to a terminal state (CANCELLED with the decision as reason, or a new REJECTED status) in `record_decision`, publishing it, so superseding applies; or make the engine record the rejection as CANCELLED instead of re-pausing.

title: Peer-set and theme-set gates cannot be passed once the operator adds a peer or theme: the page hashes the whole set, the engine and the decide pre-check hash the step's proposal only
claim: For GateKind.PEER_SET and THEME_SET, `gate_payload()` returns `peer_gate_payload(produced)` / `theme_gate_payload(produced)` — a pure function of the proposal step's frozen output — while the gate pages hash `comps.payload_for_job` / `themes.payload_for_job`, which append the operator's additions. The web decide route pre-checks the submitted hash against `gate_payload()` and returns 409 on any run with an addition; the gate step verifies against the step's own frozen `payload_hash`, so an approval carrying the page's hash never releases the run and cannot be re-taken.
evidence: vertical_slice_v1.py:3476 `return builder(produced)` with `_STEP_OUTPUT_GATES` at 3482-3483 mapping PEER_SET→`peer_gate_payload`, THEME_SET→`theme_gate_payload`; `peer_gate_payload` (2375-2377) delegates to `comps.peer_set_payload` (comps.py:142-166), which reads only `produced['peers']`. `_gate_peer_set` (2549) and `_gate_theme_set` (2662) call `_require_approval(of_step=...)` with no `expected_hash`, so the expected hash is the step's frozen one written at 2459/2607 from the step-only payload. The pages hash the whole set: pages.py:858 `payload = await peer_payload_for_job(...)` and :868 `payload_hash_for(payload)`; pages.py:920/934 likewise for themes; comps.py:388-407 `payload_for_job` appends `operator_peers_for_job` rows; themes.py:409-425 `slate_for_job` re-normalises proposal+additions. The decide route (pages.py:1775-1781) compares the form hash against `_payload_for` → `gate_payload()` (step-only) and returns 409 'The proposal changed after this page was opened'. There is an add route (pages.py:1624, 1675) and no removal route. docs/plan/acceptance-2026-09-08.md:673-678 records `payload_for_job` as 'the single funnel: the page renders it, the approval hashes it, and confirmed_* verify against it' — the engine's gate and the decide pre-check were never moved onto it. Tests: tests/test_comps_service.py:1031-1051 covers only `confirmed_peer_set`; the workflow driver (tests/run_fixtures.py:78-100) approves with `gate_payload()`, i.e. the step-only hash, and no test adds a peer/theme and then approves.
reproduction: Drive a run to gate_peer_set (a proposal with at least one peer). POST /runs/{job_id}/peers/add with a held company that has facts on or before the as-of date. GET /runs/{job_id}/peers and read the hidden payload_hash. POST /runs/{job_id}/gates/PEER_SET with that hash → 409, on every retry; the run is stuck at gate_peer_set and nothing in the GUI removes the addition. Engine path: `record_decision(payload_hash=payload_hash_for(await comps.payload_for_job(session, job_id)))` then `driver.advance(job_id)` → gate_peer_set pauses with 'recorded against different content … The page it was taken from has moved since' (context actual_hash == live_hash != approved_hash); a further decision is refused as already approved. Test to write: tests/test_run_api.py — add a peer through the page, approve through the page, assert 303 and that `driver.advance` leaves gate_peer_set.
fix_sketch: Route PEER_SET and THEME_SET in `gate_payload()` through `comps.payload_for_job` / `themes.payload_for_job`, and have `_gate_peer_set` / `_gate_theme_set` pass `expected_hash=payload_hash_for(live)` exactly as `_gate_assumptions` (1447-1463) does; then the page, the pre-check, the engine and `confirmed_*` all hash one object. Add the page-level end-to-end test above.

title: The JSON API records an approval against any 64-character hash, and can approve FINAL while the run is paused at a conditional gate or before anything is drafted
claim: `decide_gate` passes the client's `payload_hash` straight to `record_decision` without comparing it to the gate's current payload (the web route does at pages.py:1775-1781), and `_refuse_if_out_of_order` treats an undecided conditional gate as absent even when the run is paused at it. An approval recorded this way is never released by `_require_approval`, and the gate then refuses every further decision, so the run is stranded at that gate.
evidence: runs.py:372-380 — `record_decision(..., payload_hash=payload.payload_hash, ...)` with no `_payload_for` comparison; the only schema rule is 64 chars (runs.py:71). approvals.py:209 `if earlier in _CONDITIONAL and earlier not in decided: continue` — the check never consults `pending_gate` (approvals.py:233-264), which knows the run is paused at ASSUMPTIONS. runs.py:224-240 `read_draft` returns `payload_hash` for an undrafted run (the page 404s on empty content at pages.py:1041-1050; the API does not). `_require_approval` (vertical_slice_v1.py:2163-2197) then pauses; `_refuse_if_already_decided` (approvals.py:176-194) refuses a second decision. tests/test_run_api.py:426-437 only proves FINAL is refused before PLAN.
reproduction: Start a run; approve PLAN via POST /api/runs/{id}/gates/PLAN/decide with the critique_plan hash; `driver.advance` until `waiting_at == 'gate_assumptions'`. GET /api/runs/{id}/draft → a hash H0 over empty sections. POST /api/runs/{id}/gates/FINAL/decide {APPROVED, H0} → 202 (expected 422/409). Approve ASSUMPTIONS; advance to gate_final → AWAITING_APPROVAL with 'recorded against different content'; POST decide FINAL again → 422 'already approved'. Simpler: at any gate the run is paused at, POST decide with 'a'*64 → 202, then the same permanent pause.
fix_sketch: In `decide_gate`, compare `payload.payload_hash` with `payload_hash_for(await _payload_for(...))` and raise ConflictError on mismatch; in `record_decision` (or the routes) refuse a gate other than `pending_gate(job)` when the run is paused; make `read_draft` refuse an undrafted run as the page does.

title: Every stale-approval pause except the FINAL seal-drift case is a dead end: the run tells the operator to 'decide again', which `record_decision` refuses; amending an assumption after approval strands the run
claim: When the approval's hash matches neither the seal nor the live payload, `_require_approval` pauses with 'Open the review page again and decide on what it shows now', but a second decision at a decided gate is refused by `_refuse_if_already_decided`, the gate page renders the DECIDED panel with no form, and `aer reseal` acts on FINAL only. The assumptions gate is the ordinary way in: an amend or a new row after approval changes `assumptions_gate_refreshed` and the run pauses 'for a fresh decision' (the docstring's words) that cannot be taken.
evidence: vertical_slice_v1.py:2181-2184 the 'decide on what it shows now' branch; approvals.py:176-194 refuses any second decision ('changing one needs a new run'); web/gates.py:224-227 and templates/runs/_gate.html:70-77 render no form once decided; gates.py:99-108 `reseal_final_gate` re-seals FINAL only. `_gate_assumptions` docstring 1440-1442 claims 'a row changed after an approval pauses the run for a fresh decision rather than proceeding'. Amend/create routes carry no decided-gate guard: api/routes/assumptions.py:206-238 and the per-request web surface; `assumptions.propose` (services/assumptions.py:151-160) rewrites value, justification, proposed_by=actor email and confidence=None, so the original hash cannot be restored by amending back. tests/test_assumption_gate.py:1320-1330 proves the pause and stops there; nothing proves the run can then be released.
reproduction: Drive to gate_assumptions; approve on the page (or `driver.approve(..., step='propose_assumptions')`); POST /api/requests/{rid}/assumptions/{aid}/amend with a new value and reason; `driver.advance` → AWAITING_APPROVAL at gate_assumptions with the 'decide on what it shows now' message. GET /runs/{id}/assumptions → DECIDED panel, no approve form. POST /runs/{id}/gates/ASSUMPTIONS with the fresh hash → 422 'already approved'. `uv run aer reseal <id>` → 'has not sealed its final gate yet'. Resume re-pauses identically. All spend through the research wave is lost. Test to write: extend `test_a_row_amended_while_waiting_stales_the_recorded_approval` to assert a route exists that lets the operator release the run.
fix_sketch: Either give the approvals service the 'change of mind' vocabulary its docstring (approvals.py:12-14) says is missing — allow a superseding decision at a gate whose recorded approval no longer matches the live payload, keeping the old row — or refuse amend/create/add on a request whose run has already decided the relevant gate (the `refuse_settling_after_decision` pattern), and in both cases make the pause message say what is actually possible.

title: The citation override the runbook and the gate docstring promise does not exist on any surface, so an evidence pause at gate_final has no recovery
claim: `override_citation` has no caller: no web route, no API route and no CLI command writes `Citation.override_reason`. `_refuse_unsupported_evidence` runs before the approval check on every entry to gate_final and says the run is 'recoverable … by overriding a citation with a reason'; the runbook says each unverified citation 'can be overridden on the claims page'. A run that reaches gate_final with a claim whose citations do not verify (revised sections' citations are first verified here) re-pauses on every resume with the full run's spend behind it.
evidence: `grep -rn override_citation src/` finds only the definition (services/citations.py:185) and `__all__`. Claims page is GET-only (pages.py:1915) and templates/claims/detail.html:143-145 only displays an `override_reason` nothing writes; `grep override src/aer/cli.py` finds nothing relevant. vertical_slice_v1.py:2094-2096 docstring; docs/users/the-confirmation-run.md:736-737. `verify_job_citations` call sites are evaluations.py:154 (validate step, before revise) and vertical_slice_v1.py:2099 (gate_final), so citations written by the revise pass are first verified at the gate. tests/test_workflow.py:1177 proves the pause; no test proves a way out.
reproduction: Use the fixture behind tests/test_workflow.py:1151-1210 (one unsupported claim at the second gate). The run pauses at gate_final with 'claim(s) have no admissible citation' / 'citation(s) did not verify'. Open /claims/{claim_id}: no control. Search the API routers for a POST that sets `override_reason`: none. Resume → identical pause. Test to write: after the pause, drive an override through a public surface and assert the run releases — there is no surface to call.
fix_sketch: Add the claims-page form and an API route that call `override_citation` (reason required, CSRF, ownership), and a test that a run paused on evidence can be released through it; or remove the promise from the runbook and the docstring and state that such a run must be restarted.

title: Two decisions can be recorded at one gate: the already-decided check is a plain SELECT with no uniqueness rule on approvals(job_id, gate)
claim: `_refuse_if_already_decided` reads then `record_decision` inserts in the same transaction with no lock and no unique index, so two overlapping requests (a double-click, or approve then reject in quick succession) both pass and both commit. `_require_approval` and `frame_for` then read an arbitrary one of the two rows.
evidence: approvals.py:176-179 SELECT, :145 `session.add(approval)`; src/aer/db/models/approval.py:72-73 declares only two non-unique indexes and the migrations add no unique constraint on the table. vertical_slice_v1.py:2143-2149 `session.scalar(select(Approval)...)` with no ORDER BY; web/gates.py:222 `next(row for row in approvals if row.gate is gate)`. The form has two submit buttons (templates/runs/_gate.html:118-122) with no client-side disabling. The docstring's 'Approving twice is refused' is enforced only serially; tests/test_workflow.py:1015-1027 and tests/test_run_api.py:410-424 exercise sequential calls only.
reproduction: Open two sessions from the same engine; in each, run `record_decision(job, PLAN, APPROVED/REJECTED, hash)` up to `flush` without committing, then commit both. Both succeed; `approvals_for_job` returns two rows for PLAN. Then `_require_approval` releases or stops the run depending on which row Postgres returns first.
fix_sketch: A unique index on (job_id, gate) where job_id is not null, and translate the IntegrityError into the existing ValidationError; optionally disable the form's buttons on submit.

title: Nothing tests that the plan-gate estimate equals the budget guard's step table
claim: `_projected_cost` is documented as reading the same table the guard enforces 'so the number the operator approves and the number the engine enforces cannot drift apart', and today it does (Σ `build_steps()` estimates except plan, draft replaced by the spine sum when larger, plus the planner's actual spend and the pinned skills' estimate). No test asserts that relationship, so a future special-case pop or an estimate moved off the step table would silently reopen the £1.34-versus-£7.50 gap the acceptance pass found.
evidence: vertical_slice_v1.py:333-360 and the plan step at 741-752 (`agent_context.spend_gbp + _projected_cost(...)`, then `+ resolved.estimated_cost_gbp`). Existing assertions are weaker: tests/test_workflow.py:280 `plan.estimated_cost_gbp > 0`; tests/test_section_spine.py:400 `> spine_total`; tests/test_workflow.py:813-885 checks estimates exist and sum under the shipped cap, never that the gate shows their sum. `grep -rn _projected_cost tests/` finds nothing. docs/plan/acceptance-2026-09-08.md:603-606 records the fix.
reproduction: Write: `plan.estimated_cost_gbp == plan_step.cost_gbp + sum(s.estimated_cost_gbp for s in build_steps() if s.key not in {'plan','draft'}) + max(DRAFT_ESTIMATE_GBP, spine_total) + pinned_skill_estimate` against the plan row a driven run produces; it passes today and would fail on drift.
fix_sketch: Add that equality test beside `TestEveryStepThatSpendsIsOneTheGuardCanSee`.

title: Gate 1 shows the projected cost and the run's ceiling side by side but never says when the estimate already exceeds the ceiling
claim: The plan page renders 'Estimated cost of this plan £X' and the shared frame renders spend against the request's `max_cost_gbp`, but no comparison is made between the estimate and the ceiling. An operator who set a £3 cap approves a £9.31 plan with no warning, and the run then stops at the first step whose projection breaches the cap with BUDGET_EXCEEDED.
evidence: plans/review.html:178-190 shows the figure with the note 'Approving agrees to this total'; web/gates.py:250-253 `figures.cost_context(spent=state.spend_gbp, ceiling=...)` compares spend, not the estimate (figures.py:114-143). `grep -n 'ceiling\|max_cost_gbp\|exceed' plans/review.html runs/_gate.html` finds nothing. The guard pauses per step (engine.py:952-963), and `preflight.py:236-258` compares only the platform cap with the last run's cost.
reproduction: Create a request with max_cost_gbp=3, start it, open /runs/{id}/plan: estimate ≈ £9.3, frame '£0.20 of £3.00 spent', no warning; approve; the run pauses BUDGET_EXCEEDED at critique_plan or the research wave. Test: render the plan page for such a request and assert a warning element exists — none does.
fix_sketch: In the plan gate verdict block, compare `payload.estimated_cost_gbp` with the request's ceiling and say so (with the raise-cap link) when the estimate exceeds it.

title: A filer with long-term debt and no short-term-debt line is valued as debt-free (all-equity WACC, net debt = -cash)
claim: `_cost_of_capital` (lines 277-281) and `_net_debt` (lines 436-446) read only the `total_debt` concept and substitute a sourced zero when it is absent. `total_debt` is derived by `aer.calc.statements` (src/aer/calc/statements.py:360) only when BOTH `short_term_debt` and `long_term_debt` are present, and the only direct alias is the rare `DebtLongtermAndShorttermCombinedAmount` (concepts.py:275). So a balance sheet carrying `long_term_debt` but no short-term-debt tag is priced with `CapitalStructure.has_debt == False` (WACC = cost of equity, no tax shield, ALL_EQUITY_NOTE attached) and an equity bridge of EV + cash rather than EV - net debt. The same zero substitution is repeated for the comps enterprise value in src/aer/services/comps_run.py:397-407, and `cost_of_debt_required` (assumption_gate.py:493-496) mirrors it so the gate never asks for a cost of debt either. This contradicts the module's own rule that an absent line is absent, never zero, and it is silent: no caveat names the long-term debt that was ignored.
evidence: valuation_run.py:277 `debt_value = _line(latest, "total_debt", required=False)`; :281 `debt_value = Quantity.of(Decimal(0), equity_value.unit, source=equity_value.source)`; :446 `debt = Quantity.of(Decimal(0), cash.unit, source=cash.source)`. statements.py:358-362 `_DERIVED_SUMS` requires both halves. concepts.py:266-270: `ShortTermBorrowings`/`LongTermDebtCurrent` -> short_term_debt, `LongTermDebtNoncurrent`/`LongTermDebt` -> long_term_debt (the very common `DebtCurrent` is unmapped). The test fixture `a_year` (tests/assumption_fixtures.py:54) seeds `long_term_debt: "400"` with no short-term line, and tests/test_valuation_run.py:59 had to add `"short_term_debt": "0"` for the debt to be seen at all. assumption_gate.py:493-496 states in prose: 'a filer stating long-term debt alone yields no total_debt and is valued as all-equity'. No ADR or ROADMAP entry records that as a decision (grep of docs/adr and docs/plan for 'all-equity', 'total_debt', 'long-term debt alone' is empty).
reproduction: Build the tests/test_valuation_run.py scene from `a_year(...)` WITHOUT the `short_term_debt` override (i.e. long_term_debt 400, cash 300, no short-term line), confirm the same assumptions, and call `value_the_business`. Observe: `outcome.cost_of_capital.cost_of_debt_pre_tax is None`, `ALL_EQUITY_NOTE in outcome.caveats`, and the persisted `net_debt` record has output -300 while the balance sheet on the same period carries long_term_debt 400. Expected: a debt-bearing structure (net debt +100, Kd = 20/400) or a refusal naming the missing short-term line. A unit test on `_net_debt`/`_cost_of_capital` with a `PeriodAnalysis` whose statements hold only `long_term_debt` reproduces it without the database.
fix_sketch: In `_cost_of_capital`, `_net_debt`, comps_run `_inputs_for` and `cost_of_debt_required`, treat `total_debt` as absent-with-a-reason when either `long_term_debt` or `short_term_debt` is present and the sum could not be derived: raise `ValuationNotPossibleError` naming the missing half rather than substituting zero; substitute zero only when no debt line of any kind is on the statement (and say so in a caveat). Separately map `DebtCurrent` to `short_term_debt`, and add a regression test using the fixture's default (long-term-only) year.

title: DCF sensitivity-grid cells are recorded as case="base", so the football field's base band is read off grid corners

title: The DCF's working capital includes cash and short-term debt, so revenue growth is charged for accumulating cash that the net-debt bridge counts again
claim: `_working_capital` builds `opening_working_capital` as `current_assets - current_liabilities` (valuation_run.py:421-433) and the proposed `working_capital_intensity` is the mean of the same difference over revenue (assumption_proposals.py:365-380). `projected_working_capital`/`change_in_working_capital`/`free_cash_flow` (dcf.py:567-650) then deduct the year-on-year growth of that figure from FCFF. Because cash and short-term investments sit in current assets and short-term debt in current liabilities, the forecast requires the company to grow its cash pile (and shrink its short-term borrowings) in proportion to revenue and treats that as consumed cash, while the same cash is added back once in `equity_value` via net debt. The codebase already draws the operating/financing line correctly elsewhere: `quality.working_capital_intensity` (quality.py:262-268) uses trade working capital and states 'Cash, debt and tax balances are excluded because they are financing and not the operating cycle'. No ADR records the CA-CL choice for the forecast (grep of docs/adr for 'working capital' finds only ADR 0046's list of derivable drivers).

In the tests/test_valuation_run.py scene: CA 540 includes cash 300, CL 260 -> NWC 280 (28% of revenue) versus trade WC 130 (AR 150 + inventory 90 - AP 110, 13%). Year 1 at 5% growth: dWC = 1050*0.28 - 280 = 14 versus 6.5 on the trade definition, i.e. ~4% of that year's FCFF (NOPAT 207 + D&A 52.5 - capex 63) removed every year. For a cash-rich filer the effect is an order larger: Microsoft FY2023 current assets 184bn (cash + short-term investments 111bn), current liabilities 104bn, revenue 212bn -> intensity 0.38, so at 15% growth ~12bn/yr is deducted, ~7bn of it the modelled growth of the cash pile, against FCF of ~60bn.
reproduction: Compute `discounted_cash_flow` twice on the scene's inputs, once with `opening_working_capital = CA - CL` and `working_capital_intensity = 0.28`, once with `AR + inventory - AP` and `0.13`; enterprise value differs by roughly the PV of 7.5/yr growing at 5% plus its terminal capitalisation (~4% of EV in this scene). A pure test: assert that adding a sourced cash balance to `current_assets` alone lowers the DCF's equity value, which no operating change should do.
fix_sketch: Derive `working_capital_intensity` and `opening_working_capital` from trade working capital (`accounts_receivable + inventory - accounts_payable`, all already canonical concepts and already used by `quality.working_capital_intensity`), or from CA - cash - short-term investments - (CL - short-term debt); record the definition in the assumption text and the DCF assumption string.

title: The bank model's opening book value is total equity including preferred stock and non-controlling interests, divided by common shares
claim: `_inputs_from` takes `required_line(latest, "equity")` as the opening book value and `share_count` (weighted-average diluted common shares) as the divisor. `equity` is mapped from both `StockholdersEquity` and `StockholdersEquityIncludingPortionAttributableToNoncontrollingInterest` (concepts.py:279-280); when a filing tags both, the point-in-time tie-break sorts by `raw_concept` (pit.py:174), so the including-NCI figure wins. The residual-income value per share therefore includes preferred capital and minority equity in the book value attributed to each common share (~8% of book for JPM), and the proposed ROE (`net_income / equity`, assumption_proposals.py:190) is on the same inflated base with net income before preferred dividends. title: IFRS alias table names ifrs-full elements that do not exist, so a 20-F filer loses capex, share counts, SBC, taxes paid, buybacks and the debt split — and the valuation refuses

The test `test_the_concepts_with_no_ifrs_tag_are_a_recorded_decision` (tests/test_facts_schema.py:146-168) pins that only seven concepts lack an IFRS alias, i.e. asserts that capital_expenditure, share counts, SBC, taxes paid, buybacks and the debt split ARE covered — which is false in practice.
